1:
All four schools agree that these three verses belong with the chapter before them. Calvin says so and cites Dathe that the chapters are badly divided in this place, the first three verses being referable to the first; Ellicott says they form part of the previous narrative and contain its Divine purpose, which is to give the sanction of the Creator to the Sabbath — hence the ascribing of rest to him who wearies not, and hence the description of the stages of creation as days; Keil takes the heading of what follows to begin only at the generations of the heavens and of the earth.

On the host of them there are four readings and they do not agree. Clarke takes it literally as an army composed of companies under their leaders, applied to the celestial bodies ranged under the sun, and derives the name of the Sabeans from the same word because they paid divine honours to the heavenly bodies. Henry and Wesley — whose note here is an abridgement of Henry's, following it almost phrase for phrase — read the military sense morally: the creatures are numerous but marshalled, disciplined, and under command, so that every one knows and keeps his place. Ellicott denies the military sense outright: the word refers not to arrangement but to numbers gathered in crowds, sometimes the angels, oftener the stars. Calvin prefers garniture or ornament, following the Septuagint and the Vulgate against the versions in Walton, and gives the reason in an image — the heavens without sun and moon and stars would be an empty and dismantled palace, and the earth without animals and trees a poor and deserted house.

The seventh day of verse 2 is a textual crux and it splits them. Clarke reports that the Septuagint, Syriac and Samaritan read the sixth, holds that this should be considered the genuine reading, and explains the corruption mechanically: numerals were once written as letters, and vau for six is easily mistaken for zain for seven once the words were spelled out at length. Gill reports the same variant and refuses it, passing on the Jewish account that the change was made for Ptolemy king of Egypt so that he might not object that God worked on the sabbath, and arguing there is no occasion to alter the text. Ellicott gives a third explanation, that the substitution was made to avoid even the appearance of Elohim putting the finishing touches to creation on the Sabbath.

What the resting was, three of them settle the same way. Henry, Calvin and Ellicott all deny that God ceased to work, since the Father worketh hitherto and, as Calvin puts it, if God withdrew his hand a little all things would perish; what ceased was the creation of new kinds. Henry adds that in miracles God has overruled nature but never changed its settled course, and that he rested not as one weary but as one well pleased.

On the blessing, Clarke works from the word, which means to speak good of or to, so that God has spoken well of the Sabbath and good to those who keep it. Calvin makes sanctified exegetical of blessed: to sanctify is to separate from the common number. Ellicott presses the order of the words — the blessing was given before any covenant and by Elohim, the God of nature, not Jehovah, so the weekly rest is universal, permanent, and independent of the Mosaic law; and he notes on Sayce's authority that the Accadians observed a sabbath, though tied to the sun, moon and planets. Gill reads the verse proleptically instead, and reports Jarchi referring the blessing forward to the manna.
4:
Verse 4 is read as a hinge, and the question is what it hinges. Gill takes the generations to look backward: the preceding account is a history of the production of the heavens and earth, creation being a kind of generation and the day of it a sort of birthday. Keil takes it forward, and insists that what follows is not a second and independent history of the creation, nor a set of appendices to the first, but the commencement of the history of the human race, describing the place God prepared for man's abode. Ellicott handles the phrase in the day by observing that the six days, viewed with reference to the weekly rest, are here described as one, because they were divisions in one continuous act.

The change of the divine name is noticed by everyone and explained by no two alike. Henry marks that the first chapter has only Elohim, a God of power, and that here we get Jehovah Elohim, a God of power and perfection, a finishing God, the name being given when the work is perfected as it was given when he performed his promise. Wesley follows him and glosses the name as meaning he that was, and is, and is to come. Calvin reports the inference some have drawn from the distribution of the names — that the early Mosaic history is older than Moses, who arranged fragments of primeval annals into one narrative — and sets against it the argument that each passage requires the very appellation used and no other, allowing the distinction importance without granting the theory. Ellicott simply notes Jehovah-Elohim and refers the reader to an excursus. Clarke turns aside from the Hebrew to the English word Lord, which he derives from the Anglo-Saxon for loaf and for supplying, so that a lord is a dispenser of bread as the old nobility were who kept open house; and he applies it to him who is the bread of God which cometh down from heaven.

On the plants of verse 5 the readings diverge sharply. Ellicott corrects the translation: not that God created vegetation, but that no wild shrub was yet on the earth and no herb had sprung up, the writer preparing for the planting of paradise — and geology teaches the literal truth of it, since while the earth was hot enough for water to exist only as vapour there could be no vegetation. Calvin explains the repetition differently: the herbs made on the third day are named again so that we may know they were then produced unlike what we now see — no seed, no root, nothing grafted or shooting, but each springing at God's command, with a durable vigour needing neither rain nor culture. Clarke agrees that everything was created in full maturity, so that man found all ready for his use. Gill makes the narrower point that the plants were made before any were planted or any seed sown, and so were the immediate production of divine power.

Henry draws the practical inferences: the earth did not bring forth by any innate virtue of its own; rain is a gift, and it is God who causes it to rain upon one city and not upon another; and though God ordinarily works by means he is not tied to them, so that we must not tempt God in the neglect of means but must trust him in the want of them. On the mist Clarke offers a meteorological account — vapours ascending, condensing in colder air, falling back as dew, which he thinks is Moses teaching how rain is produced; Gill has the vapour rise once the waters were drained and the earth warmed; and Ellicott, on the strength of the same word rendered vapour in Job, calls the mist the measure and material of rain.
7:
On the forming of man the note everyone takes is the word itself. Gill says the verb is the potter's and the matter red earth mixed with water, which humbles pride: man is dust, and to dust he returns. Ellicott makes the point structurally: the prominent idea here is not producing out of nothing but shaping, so that where Elohim is almighty power Jehovah is wisdom and skill, and the whole narrative is anthropomorphic, showing a God who forms and builds and plants. The material marks feebleness — not rock nor ore but the light shifting particles of the surface.

Then they divide over living soul. Ellicott says the word carries no idea of spiritual existence, since the animals bear the same phrase in the first chapter, and puts man's superiority in the manner of the bestowal; he insists only that the life came as a direct gift and not by evolution. Calvin, against most of the ancients, reaches the same conclusion independently — the words describe the lower faculty which imparts breath and motion — while maintaining that the human soul keeps its proper rank. Clarke takes the opposite view, building on the plural breath of lives, animal and intellectual, so that the inspiration gave both spirit and understanding and body and soul are distinct things. Calvin finds man's dignity elsewhere: the beasts arose out of the earth in a moment, but man was gradually formed.

The garden is located four ways and none agree. Gill puts Eden in Mesopotamia and reads eastward as possibly before, the planting having been on the third day. Keil takes Eden as delight, the proper name of a district not to be confused with the Eden of Assyria or Coelesyria, and traces Paradise through the Septuagint to a Persian word for a hedged enclosure that reached Hebrew through Solomon's commerce. Clarke agrees Eden is a place though the word means pleasure, and derives the gardens of the Hesperides and of Adonis from it, but leaves the etymology of paradise uncertain. Ellicott denies that eastward means the eastern portion of Eden — flatly against Keil at the same phrase — holding that Eden lay east of the regions known to Israel, and that the flood so altered the ground that the four rivers cannot be identified. Both converge on one point, that the rendering in the beginning is untenable; and Calvin adds that the garden was one region, not the whole world as some authors would have it.

Henry and Wesley describe the place instead. It was a garden, not an ivory house: as clothes came in with sin, so did houses; heaven was the roof, earth the floor, and the shadow of the trees his rooms, which Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like. Both add that the penman writes for the infant church by outward appearances, the Mosaic history having the patterns of heavenly things rather than the heavenly things themselves.

On the two trees the division is sharpest. Clarke reads the tree of life first as the medicinal plants that keep death at a distance, then as the means of preserving the body in continual vital energy, an antidote against death. Ellicott says the same, that its continual use would have kept a naturally mortal body alive for ever, and argues the other tree can only have got its name after the fall, since innocence could not know evil without feeling or seeing it. Calvin refuses the physical construction: the tree was so named not because it could confer life but as a symbol and memorial of life already received, God being accustomed to attest his grace by external symbols; whether two trees or two kinds are meant he thinks not worth contending over. Gill adds that the trees gratified sight as well as taste, and makes them an emblem of the saints.
10:
Clarke opens by measuring the wreckage. It would astonish an ordinary reader, he says, to see the variety of opinions on where paradise stood: in the third heaven or the fourth, within the moon's orbit or in the moon itself, at either pole, in Tartary, China, Ceylon, Armenia, Africa under the equator, Mesopotamia, Persia, Arabia, Assyria, Palestine, Europe — or nowhere, being invisible or merely spiritual. He refuses that last: the description is too particular to be understood allegorically, and one might as well make Adam and Eve allegorical as their address. He then adopts Reland's reconstruction, placing it in Armenia near the sources of the Euphrates, Tigris, Phasis and Araxes, identifying Pison with the Phasis of Colchis because the city Chabala answers to Havilah, and Gihon with the Araxes because both names mean rapid motion.

Calvin is more interested in method than in a site. He blocks the easy escape first: some say the deluge changed the surface of the globe and shifted the springs, and he will not accept it — the earth was cursed and in places laid waste, but it is still the same earth created in the beginning. What he grants instead is that Moses accommodated his topography to the capacity of his age, and speaks not philosophically but popularly, as he called the moon one of two great luminaries not because it is larger but because it looks so. Hence the four heads are not four springs — no fountain is mentioned, only one river — but the streams above and the mouths below a confluence, the Euphrates having once joined the Tigris; and he marshals Pliny on the Orcheni who drew off the Euphrates through their lands, and Nearchus reckoning three thousand three hundred stadia from its mouth to Babylon, before submitting an actual map to the reader.

Ellicott reads the tenses as present, as though the features of the country were unchanged: a river goes forth from Eden, and outside the garden is parted into four main streams. This has made many put the site in a submerged part of the Persian Gulf, where the Babylonian legends place it, at Eridu below the junction of the Tigris and Euphrates, with the Indus and Nile for the other two; and Rawlinson has suggested the province of Gan-duniyas instead. He objects to both on a single ground — from either the ark could not have floated against the current of the flood up to the highlands of Armenia. And he records without endorsing that many authors have taken the passage symbolically, one Syriac writer reading it as a description of the human body.

Gill works name by name and keeps his options open. What the one river was is hard to say: the Euphrates and Tigris where they met is the general view, though one learned man holds it now lost and another makes it the Jordan. Pison he denies to be the Nile, against the rabbinic derivation from a word for spreading, and denies to be the Ganges, against Josephus, since the country described suits neither Egypt nor India; he prefers the river the ancients called Phasis or Physcus, a branch of the Pasitigris. On the gold he brings Diodorus, who reports an Arabian gold called apyrus that needs no fire but comes from the ground pure and in pieces the size of chestnuts, so bright that jewellers set precious stones in it; and Strabo, for the gold-bearing rivers of Colchis, whence the fable of the golden fleece — the same fable Clarke reaches from Havilah. Clarke closes on the two hard words, reporting the guess that bdellium is the pearl-oyster and shoham the onyx, named from the Greek for a fingernail because of its colour, then declining to decide: it is impossible to say what the originals mean, and at this distance it is of little consequence.
13:
Gihon is claimed by four candidates and Gill will not choose. One of the name flowed near Jerusalem, which suits the opinion that Eden lay in Israel; Josephus makes it the Nile; it looks to him like a branch of the Euphrates or Tigris on the east; and Reland makes it the Araxes. He derives the name from coming forth with great force — and then, in the same breath, has it pour itself into the Baltic sea, which fits none of the four. Ellicott disposes of the Nile by a historical rather than a geographical argument: it was proposed because Gihon compasses Cush, but Cush then meant southern Arabia, and only later did colonists carry the name to Abyssinia. He adds that Gihon is a common Arabic word for a river, offers the Oxus, and reports Sayce preferring the Araxes.

On Hiddekel the two work opposite ways. Gill collects the etymology — Diglath in the Targum, the Diglito of Pliny, Tigris from the swiftness of the tiger or the Persian word for a dart, Hiddekel itself meaning sharp and swift like a polished arrow — then lets modern travellers contradict it: the river is slower than the Euphrates, very crooked, and choked with islands and banks of stone. Ellicott attacks the form of the word instead. Hiddekel is startling as a quadriliteral; the Samaritan Codex reads it with the article, which he thinks probably right, though Sayce keeps the received reading and takes the first syllable for the Accadian for river. Of the Euphrates he argues from silence: no description is given because it was the largest and best known of Asiatic rivers, from which it probably follows that Pison and Gihon were small streams.

At the placing of the man Gill is careful about the verb used. It is not a corporeal assumption but a leading by the hand — the Targum has simply that he led him, a rabbinic paraphrase that he took him with good words and persuaded him. He passes on the traditions that Adam was made near Damascus, or where the temple afterwards stood. Ellicott notices that the narrative has come back to the earlier verse with a different word: here it means he made him rest, giving the garden as a permanent dwelling.

Three schools then draw the same conclusion from the two verbs, and one adds a shadow. Calvin holds that men were created to employ themselves in work and not to lie down in idleness; the labour was pleasant and exempt from weariness, but in Adam's person God condemned all indolent repose, nothing being more contrary to the order of nature than to consume life in eating, drinking and sleeping. Clarke says gardening is the first employment on record, undertaken in innocence, and that man could not have been happy inactive: his body as well as his mind proves he was never meant for a merely contemplative life. Henry shuts out boasting first — only he that made us can make us happy — and then argues that those who do their earthly business with an eye to God serve him as truly as when they are upon their knees, the husbandman's calling being honourable since it was needful even in paradise. Calvin alone turns the second verb into stewardship: to be given custody of a thing is to hold it on condition of frugal use and care for what remains, so that a man should hand his field to posterity as he received it or better cultivated, neither dissipating it by luxury nor letting it be ruined by neglect. Ellicott alone hears a warning in it. The word to keep implies difficulty and danger; though no blight spoiled the crop, the garden had to be guarded against wild animals and birds, and protected against the violence of winds and the burning heat of the sun.
16:
Everyone reads the single prohibition as a test rather than a dietary rule. Calvin puts it bluntly: it would have made no difference to God what fruit Adam ate, so the prohibition was a test of obedience, a first lesson by which man might know he had a Lord on whose will he depended. He then meets Paul head-on. If the law is not made for the righteous, what need had innocent Adam of one? Paul, he answers, argues from the common practice of life — those who run freely need no compulsion — and does not deny that God imposed a law from the beginning to maintain his own right; if the law is called a minister of death, it is so accidentally, through our corruption. Clarke calls it the first positive precept and proof of a probationary state: man was lord of this world but only God's vicegerent, and one from whose mind that dependence is erased is capable of any wickedness. An intelligent creature without a law, he adds, is an absurdity. Henry places the weight on who was commanded: Adam stood as a public person, the father and representative of all mankind, receiving law as he had lately received a nature. Gill observes that the Creator and preserver had the right to command, and that the prohibition bound the woman too, though her making is related later.

On the sentence they divide over how quickly it fell. Clarke translates literally, dying thou shalt die, taking it both ways: spiritual death by the loss of the life of God, and mortality from that moment, so that every moment of life is an act of dying. Wesley says the same, adding the loss of all happiness in possession or in prospect. Henry reads the positive half of the grant as an assurance of immortal life, the tree of life standing in the midst of the garden and being the one thing withdrawn at the revolt.

The declaration that it is not good for man to be alone is expounded four ways. Henry pities the solitude: an upper world of angels and a lower world of brutes, and none of his own rank between, so that perfect solitude would turn a paradise into a desert and a palace into a dungeon — two being better than one. God could have made a world of men at once, as he replenished heaven with angels, but chose a succession beginning from two. Wesley reproduces the first observation almost word for word. Calvin generalises beyond Adam: the commencement involves a general principle, that man was formed a social animal, and solitude is not good for anyone God does not exempt by special privilege — which he turns against those who think celibacy advantageous, heathen writers and Jerome alike. Clarke reaches the same verdict from the vocabulary: celibacy is not good on either side, and men may call it a state of excellence but the word of God says the reverse.

What the helper is produces the one flat contradiction. Clarke construes the phrase as one like himself, standing opposite to him, and concludes the woman a perfect resemblance with neither inferiority nor superiority, in all things like and equal. Ellicott, from the same words, draws the declaration that the female is subsequent in order of production to the male and formed from him, though the first chapter makes male and female simultaneous; and he grounds the happiness of marriage not on her being the same as the man but on his seeing in her his counterpart. Keil takes the word to mean a helping being in which the man may recognise himself, and observes that such help was needed for his whole calling, to govern the earth and not merely to multiply. Gill notes that the saying was a purpose in God's own mind, formed on the sixth day.
19:
The order of these verses is the first difficulty. Ellicott says much curious speculation has come of mistaking it for chronology, as though the animals were made after man and woman called into being only when they had all failed him; the real point is what it shows of Adam's intellectual condition, the assertion that woman alone is meet for him coming last and with cumulative force. Calvin makes the same grammatical point, that the verb refers to what had already taken place, and adds that none of the animals was found adapted to Adam, and not through ignorance, since he named them from certain knowledge.

How the naming happened, they describe incompatibly. Calvin takes the bringing to mean that God endued the creatures with a disposition to obedience, so that they voluntarily offered themselves to be inspected; and he infers that such gentleness would have remained in wild beasts had Adam not forfeited his authority, whereas now some are tamed with difficulty and some inspire terror. He notes that only the animals nearest man are spoken of. Ellicott denies the procession outright: not a long train of beasts and birds passing before the man to receive each its title, but a keen observer who meets new creatures as he works, studies their ways, and at length names them — most names being imitations of their cries or taken from some feature of form, plumage or motion. Clarke takes the opposite view of the knowledge involved: the names in Scripture always express some essential characteristic, and without intuitive knowledge of those properties Adam could never have given them — a strong proof of his original perfection. Gill adds that the creatures were made two and two, man single.

On the sleep, Gill insists it was supernatural and not natural weariness, the senses so locked that he felt nothing, both that the operation might be painless and that he might have no hand in the woman's formation. Henry adds another reason: Adam slept so that no room might be left to imagine he had directed the Spirit of the Lord or been his counsellor; and while he knows no sin God will take care he shall feel no pain. Wesley repeats both sentences almost unchanged.

What was taken, and what follows from it, divides them sharply. Ellicott points out that the word is never rendered rib except here but always side or flank, as the ancient versions all have it: woman was not made from one of many ribs whose loss a man would not feel, but is one side of him. Clarke thinks it immaterial whether rib or side is read: God could have formed her from the dust as he formed the man, but then she would have appeared a distinct being to whom he had no natural relation, whereas being of the same flesh and blood she has, he says, equal powers, faculties and rights. Henry reasons the other way from the same order — Adam was first formed, then Eve, made of the man and for the man, urged as grounds of submissiveness — yet balances it: being made after him and out of him puts an honour on the sex, for if man is the head she is the crown, and the man was dust refined where the woman was dust double-refined. Calvin answers the scoffers, who think the account fabulous or object that the rib was superfluous and its loss a mutilation. His conjecture is that something was taken so that Adam might embrace a part of himself the more warmly, losing a rib and gaining a richer reward; the deeper reason being that both sexes spring from one origin, so that he might recognise himself in his wife as in a mirror and she submit willingly as taken out of him, where different origins would have bred contempt and contention.
22:
The verb at verse 22 is not the one used before, and both who notice it build on it. Gill observes that she was neither created out of nothing nor formed of dust but built, a word suiting her as the foundation of the family; and she was taken not from a superior part nor an inferior but from the side, near the heart, to be loved and kept. Ellicott presses it further: her formation required time and care, so that woman is no casual production of nature but the finished result of labour and skill, brought with honour as the Creator's last and most perfect work, and made not from the ground but from the man. Calvin draws from the verse that marriage is divinely instituted, since Adam did not take a wife at his own will but received her as offered by God; and he names two contrary artifices by which Satan defames it: the odium that introduces the pestilential law of celibacy, and the licence married persons claim.

The exclamation raises two questions. How did Adam know, being asleep? Calvin refuses the answer that quickness of perception let him guess, and concludes that God revealed both the fact and its design, the sleep having been sent not to hide the woman's origin but to spare him pain. Wesley thinks it was shown him in a vision. The second is what this now means. Clarke renders it this turn, this creature which now passes before me, tying it to the creatures already passed and found unsuitable. Ellicott takes it for a beat of the foot in keeping time, hence at last, and notes that bone stands for self in the Semitic dialects, so that the phrase means my very own self. Wesley notes that her name is a feminine of the word for man, a she-man differing from him in sex only, not in nature.

Who speaks verse 24 is genuinely disputed. Gill reports that some take it for Moses inferring and others for Adam under inspiration, but judges it God's own, Christ quoting it as the saying of their Maker. Ellicott says the opposite — they are evidently the narrator's, since Adam knew nothing of young men leaving home — and reconciles the quotation by holding the narrator moved by the Spirit. Calvin weighs all three and approves that Moses added it as teacher; Wesley inclines to Adam speaking in God's name. Calvin's use of it is severe: the husband must prefer his wife even to his father, so that they who allow divorce for slight causes overturn the laws of nature. He and Clarke converge on the reading they two shall be one flesh, Calvin from the singular used throughout, Clarke from the versions, which he thinks preserve a word a copyist struck from the wrong verse; without the numeral a man might claim as many wives as he chooses.

The last verse is read forward by one, inward by another. Ellicott insists it is not the close of the marriage section, where it would be indelicate, but the introduction to the temptation, and points to the play by which man is arom, naked, the serpent arum, crafty. Calvin turns it into a question about ourselves: nakedness disgraces nothing in an ass or an ox, yet we cannot look on a naked man without shame, and each is ashamed of his own with no witness by. Where then is the dignity in which we excel? In uncorrupted nature, he answers, there was nothing but what was honourable, so whatever is now opprobrious must be imputed to our own fault. Clarke grounds the absence of shame in the absence of sin, shame arising only from consciousness of irregular conduct; and Wesley puts it best: blushing is now the colour of virtue, but it was not the colour of innocency.
